content:
Mutah is a fixed-term marriage contract, and Muslims disagree about it more sharply than about almost any other question of family law. Critics say Islam allows prostitution under another name. Some Muslims say the Quran still permits it.

The contract has a precise shape. A man and a woman agree a marriage for a stated period and a stated dower; when the period ends, the marriage ends without divorce; the woman then observes a waiting period before she may marry again; and in Twelver Shia law, which permits the contract, a child born of it is legitimate and inherits from both parents. The Sunni schools hold it forbidden. The disagreement between the two positions is old and serious, and it is a dispute among Muslims about their own sources, so it deserves to be read in those sources.

The reports reach us in the canonical hadith collections, and the great commentators gathered them in one place. These six points follow that record.

Two passages in the Quran describe the believers as those who guard their private parts except from their wives and "what their right hands possess" (23:5-6 and 70:29-31).[1] Surah al-Nisa then lists the women a man may marry and says: fa-mastamtatum bihi minhunna fa-atuhunna ujurahunna faridatan ("so for whatever you have enjoyed of them, give them their dower as an obligation") in 4:24.

The question is what istamtatum means in that verse. Al-Tabari collects the early reports and records that Ibn Abbas read the word as ordinary marriage: once a man marries a woman and has intercourse with her, her whole dower is owed.[2]

The verses on guarding chastity add a further step, used by Sunni jurists. They limit lawful intimacy to wives and those whom the right hand possesses, and continue: "whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors."[1] A woman in a temporary contract, the jurists argued, lacks the marks the law attaches to a wife: the spouses do not inherit from each other by default, and the marriage ends without divorce. On this reasoning she falls outside the two permitted categories.[3] Twelver scholars reply that she is a wife in a particular kind of contract, and that the rules on inheritance and divorce differ between kinds of marriage without making the contract unlawful.

Other reports in al-Tabari give the verse as "for whatever you have enjoyed of them for a fixed term" (ila ajalin musamman). They name Ibn Abbas, Ubayy ibn Kab and Qatada, and Abu Nadra says that Ibn Abbas insisted three times that God sent the verse down that way.[4] That wording is not in the Quran as it was written in the Uthmani copies and recited by the community. Al-Tabari himself reads the verse as one about marriage and the settling of the dower, and he calls the explanation of al-Suddi, who took it as a fixed-term contract, a view with no meaning.[5]

The disagreement therefore begins with a variant that a few early authorities held and that the text everyone recites does not contain.

Twelver Shia commentators read the verse the other way. Al-Tabarsi, the twelfth-century author of Majma al-Bayan, takes istamtatum as a reference to the temporary contract and cites the variant reading of Ibn Abbas and Ubayy in support.[6] A fair account has to record that the variant was held by respected Companions. The question is what weight a reading outside the recited text can carry in law, and on that the Sunni schools hold that it carries none on its own.

Abdullah ibn Masud reports that the Companions fought beside the Prophet without their wives, and asked whether they should castrate themselves. The Prophet forbade it.[7] Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani places the permission in the same setting: the men were far from home, the strain of living unmarried was heavy, and the Prophet allowed them to contract a marriage for a set period.[8]

Jabir ibn Abdullah and Salama ibn al-Akwa say that a herald of the Prophet came to them and announced that they were allowed to do so.[9] Salama adds that the allowance covered three nights, after which the couple could separate or extend.[10]

The setting matters for understanding the permission. The Arabs before Islam knew several kinds of union, some of them barely distinguishable from prostitution, and the Quran and the Prophet set out to bring sexual life within marriage. A fixed-term contract with a dower and a waiting period was, in that setting, a step towards regulation. The reports place it among men on campaign, far from their wives, as a concession to hardship.

Ali ibn Abi Talib reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet forbade mutah and the meat of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar.[11] Sabra al-Juhani reports in Muslim that the Prophet stood and said he had permitted mutah before, and that God had now forbidden it until the Day of Resurrection. Anyone with such a woman was to release her and keep what he had given.[12]

Ibn Hajar counts six occasions that the reports name: Khaybar, the umra of the following year, the conquest of Mecca, Awtas, Tabuk and the farewell pilgrimage. He weighs each chain and finds the firm ones to be Khaybar and the conquest. He gives the weak reasons for the rest, for instance the mursal report of al-Hasan al-Basri about the umra and a chain through Abbad ibn Kathir, whom he calls matruk (abandoned), for Tabuk.[13]

Some Sunni scholars read the Khaybar report more narrowly. Ibn al-Qayyim argued that Ali's report joins two separate statements, and that what was forbidden at Khaybar was the meat of domestic donkeys, while the prohibition of mutah came at the conquest of Mecca.[14] On his reading the timeline is simpler, and the decisive ban is the one in Sabra's report, "until the Day of Resurrection". The Sunni conclusion does not depend on which reading of the Khaybar report is correct.

Al-Nawawi, in Ibn Hajar's summary, holds that mutah was allowed before Khaybar, forbidden there, allowed again in the year of the conquest, and then forbidden for good. Al-Shafii is quoted as saying the same, that it was abrogated twice.[15] Al-Mawardi gives two readings: either the ban was repeated so that more people heard it, or the permission was renewed. Ibn Hajar prefers the second, because the last statement says "until the Day of Resurrection", wording that closes the matter in a way the earlier bans did not.[15]

Both explanations agree on the outcome. The final statement came at the conquest, and no permission followed it.

Ibn Umar reports in Ibn Majah that when Umar became caliph he stood and said that the Messenger of God had permitted mutah for three days and then forbidden it.[16] Ibn Hajar draws the conclusion that Umar was not making a ruling of his own. He cited a prohibition of the Prophet, and the Companions did not contradict him.[16]

Some people had carried on after the Prophet because they had not heard of the ban. Jabir mentions that practice up to Umar's time.[16]

Shia scholars read Umar's announcement differently. They cite a report in which Umar says that two kinds of mutah were practised in the Prophet's time and that he forbids them and will punish those who practise them, and they take it as evidence that the ban was his own decision.[17] Sunni scholars reply that the same Umar, in the report of Ibn Majah, attributed the ban to the Prophet, and that the Companions present, Ali among them, did not object, as they did on other occasions when they thought Umar mistaken. The two readings of Umar's words are the heart of the historical dispute.

Ibn Abbas is reported in al-Bukhari to have allowed mutah. A freedman of his answered that this was in a time of hardship when women were few, and Ibn Abbas agreed.[18] Ali, according to Muslim, rebuked him for his lenience and told him that the Prophet had forbidden it at Khaybar.[19] Ibn Battal says the reports of Ibn Abbas's retraction have weak chains, and that his permission is the better attested.[20]

Ibn al-Mundhir, quoted by Ibn Hajar, found no one who allowed it in his own time except some of the Shia. Al-Khattabi adds that the Shia position does not fit their own rule of turning to Ali and his family, since Ali's report of abrogation is sound.[20] Al-Bayhaqi reports, through al-Khattabi, that Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about it and called it zina itself.[20] I have not checked that attribution against Shia sources. A reader who wants the Twelver case should read it from those sources, and read the Sunni reports above alongside it. Iyad, quoted by Ibn Hajar, records a consensus of all other scholars against it.[20]

Shia scholars have a pointed reply to modern Sunni practice. Some Sunni jurists today permit forms of marriage in which the wife waives rights to housing and maintenance, or in which the husband privately intends to divorce after a period, and Shia writers ask how these differ from a temporary contract that at least states its term openly.[21] Sunni scholars are themselves divided on those modern forms. The argument shows that the underlying questions, of protection for women and honesty about the terms of a marriage, are live on both sides.

The bottom line

The sources show a permission given for a short period to men on campaign, followed by prohibition, with the last statement placed at the conquest of Mecca. The contrary reading of 4:24 depends on a variant that the recited text does not contain. The question to ask of any modern claim is whether it accounts for Ali's report and for the announcement of Umar.

The critic's charge, that Islam permits prostitution under another name, fails on either side of the Muslim debate. The Sunni majority holds the contract forbidden. The Twelver Shia, who permit it, attach to it a dower, a waiting period, the legitimacy of children and the rules of kinship, which no commercial transaction carries. Muslims disagree about whether the permission was ended. They agree that sexual relations belong within a contract recognised by the law.

Notes

  1. Quran 23:5-6 and 70:29-31. For the meaning of 4:24 see al-Tabari, Jami al-bayan (Dar al-Tarbiya edition), vol. 8, pp. 175-181.
  2. Al-Tabari, Jami al-bayan, vol. 8, p. 175, report no. 9028 (Ibn Abbas, through Ali ibn Abi Talha).
  3. Ibn Qudama, al-Mughni, Book of Marriage, section on the marriage of mutah.
  4. Al-Tabari, Jami al-bayan, vol. 8, pp. 176-178, reports nos. 9035-9042 (Ibn Abbas, Ubayy ibn Kab, Qatada) and report no. 9033 (al-Suddi).
  5. Al-Tabari, Jami al-bayan, vol. 8, pp. 180-181. He lists the views on the clause "and there is no blame on you in what you agree upon after the obligation", prefers the reading about settling the dower, and rejects al-Suddi's explanation.
  6. Al-Fadl ibn al-Hasan al-Tabarsi, Majma al-Bayan fi Tafsir al-Quran, commentary on Quran 4:24.
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 5071 (Book of Marriage, chapter on the marrying of a poor man), narrated by Ibn Masud.
  8. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 9, p. 170, where he recalls Ibn Masud's report of why the permission was given.
  9. Sahih Muslim 1405a (Book of Marriage, chapter on mutah, its permission, its abrogation and its prohibition until the Day of Resurrection), narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah and Salama ibn al-Akwa. Al-Bukhari reports it as 5117-5118.
  10. Sahih al-Bukhari 5119, the report of Salama ibn al-Akwa on the three nights. See Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, p. 167. Muslim 1406a records a related report from Sabra al-Juhani, who stayed three nights before the Prophet told the men to release the women.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 5115 and 4216, narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talib (chapters on the Prophet's prohibition of mutah, and the expedition of Khaybar).
  12. Sahih Muslim 1406d, narrated by Sabra al-Juhani through his son al-Rabi. Ibn Hajar's own discussion of the report is in Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, pp. 169-170.
  13. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, pp. 168-170 (the six occasions, and his assessment of each).
  14. Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, Zad al-Ma'ad, section on the expedition of Khaybar and on the rulings of the conquest of Mecca.
  15. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, p. 170, quoting al-Nawawi, al-Shafii and al-Mawardi (al-Hawi).
  16. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, p. 172, on Umar's announcement, citing Ibn Majah, and the later practice reported by Jabir.
  17. The report "two mutahs were practised in the time of the Messenger of God", attributed to Umar, as cited by Twelver scholars; compare al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra, Book of Marriage.
  18. Sahih al-Bukhari 5116, narrated by Abu Jamra, who heard Ibn Abbas asked about the mutah of women.
  19. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, p. 168, collecting the reports that Ali rebuked Ibn Abbas. Muslim reports the version in which Ali tells him to be gentle and cites the ban at Khaybar.
  20. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, vol. 9, p. 173, quoting Ibn Battal, Ibn al-Mundhir, Iyad, al-Khattabi and al-Bayhaqi.
  21. On the modern debate over misyar marriage and marriage with an undisclosed intention of divorce, see Shahla Haeri, Law of Desire: Temporary Marriage in Shi'i Iran, rev. ed. (Syracuse: Syracuse University Press, 2014).
